https://www.dw.com/en/haiti-un-chief-con.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JO7X Survivors of the attack fled with whatever belongings they could carry Image: Patrice Noel/REUTERS Advertisement At least 47 people, including at least five children, were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped by armed men in Haiti on Sunday, the United Nations confirmed on Tuesday. The incident, which took place in Kenscoff on the outskirts of the capital, Port-au-Prince, is believed to be one of the largest mass kidnappings in the troubled Caribbean country in recent years. In a video posted on social media, a gang leader threatened to murder hostages if Haiti's National Police kill any of his men in an attempt to rescue people. "If any of our soldiers are hurt, I will kill all of them," he said. One resident told the Associated Press that gang members had kidnapped his brother, stepmother, stepfather and two cousins. He said his 16-year-old niece was also kidnapped and raped but managed to escape. "I had to run over bodies," he said, recalling his own escape. "I can't sleep knowing all these people died." Haiti: UN condemns violence United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres condemned the attack which he said underscored the "alarming security conditions" in Haiti and amplified the need for both domestic and international security efforts. Via a spokesman, he called for Haitian authorities to "ensure that those responsible for such attacks are held accountable," including through specialized judicial units recently established with international support to investigate mass crimes. How the West messed with Haiti To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Strategic location targeted by gangs Kenscoff is located around 10 kilometers south of Port-au-Prince at an altitude of around 2,000 meters. Thanks to its cooler climate, is considered a relatively desirable residential area, while its mountainous location also makes it strategically important when it comes to control of key road connections. Kenscoff is also close to the political institutions, embassies and banks of Pétion-Ville, a comparatively affluent suburb of the capital. The first major attack on Kenscoff occurred in January 2025. Since then, there have been sporadic attacks in the mountains surrounding the city center. But Sunday's attack was the largest yet, shattering the belief that security in the Caribbean country was improving. Haiti: 'Major security test for government' "This is a major political and security test for the government, for the police and for the international mission," said Romain Le Cour, head of the Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime. Le Cour believes the threat of executing hostages is a trap: if the authorities don't act, they will be seen to be abandoning the captives; but if they do and more people die, the gangs will blame the state. More than 3,050 people were reported to have been killed in Haiti between January to June, according to UN statistics released this week, while gang violence has displaced an estimated 1.5 million more. The UN also noted that nearly 800 rapes and over 80 kidnappings were reported between April and June alone. "These figures represent only a portion of the total number of people kidnapped," read a statement, pointing out that victims' relatives often choose to negotiate directly with the kidnappers in the belief that this approach will secure a quicker release and avoid possible reprisals. https://www.dw.com/en/at-least-four-dead.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ORdN The rain and flooding has devastated several communities along Spain's eastern coast Image: Jose Jordan/AFP Advertisement At least four people have died after heavy rain and severe flooding across eastern Spain , forcing hundreds of people to flee. The worst-affected areas are in the Valencia and Alicante regions, on Spain's eastern Mediterranean coast. In the town of Oliva, two bodies were recovered on Monday. One victim was a 79-year-old woman found at her home, while another was a man who died from a heart attack at a campsite. In Sagunto, a man drowned while swimming at the beach, while in Catalonia, a woman died after falling into a rain-swollen stream in Catalonia. Emergency services have rescued more than 450 people who were stranded by the rising water. Some had to be airlifted from rooftops, flooded buildings and vehicles, while others were brought to safety by boat. Roads were underwater on Monday Image: Rober Solsona/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance Residents use buckets to drain water from their homes in Daimuz Image: Ana Beltran/REUTERS Pile of furniture on a muddy street Image: Rober Solsona/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance Emergency restrictions Authorities imposed emergency restrictions across several municipalities, asking people to stay indoors. Most restrictions have since been lifted. The Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean, including Mallorca and Ibiza, were also affected, with schools closed, and some flights cancelled or delayed. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said military emergency teams were assisting with the rescue efforts and pledged full government support. The latest flooding comes almost two years after the Valencia region suffered a devastating flood disaster that killed more than 220 people. https://www.politico.eu/article/estonias.text: TALLINN — Imagine French General Charles de Gaulle, exiled in London during World War II, running his Free France government by logging into the cloud. Officials in Estonia are preparing for exactly such a scenario with a new strategy to boost doomsday resilience — hukukindlus in Estonian — that would allow the government’s digital services to be run entirely from abroad if its territory is occupied by a foreign enemy. The Baltic country of 1.3 million, which shares a 294-kilometer border with Russia, fears it is a prime target if Moscow were to invade a European Union country. Security services have already warned that Russia is waging a hybrid war on Europe, and Estonia has blamed Moscow for everything from cyberattacks to arson plots to cuts to undersea data cables . Advertisement Advertisement Now, Tallinn is preparing to move its public services to the cloud “either when data centers are destroyed or there’s boots on the ground and we cannot operate,” said Tõnu Grünberg, an architect of the new strategy and former deputy secretary general for digital infrastructure and cybersecurity at Estonia's Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs. Estonia already has a data backup in its “digital embassy” in Luxembourg , effectively a copy of the country's blueprint that includes everything from citizen registries to land registries and its legal code. “Now we want to really be online, whatever happens,” Grünberg said. "All critical services stay online … Everything needs to stay operational.” The Estonian government is building secure applications on cloud providers including Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services as well as its own state cloud platform. The country is shipping the system to its data embassy and other places in Europe, said Grünberg, who started a job as CEO of tech infrastructure provider Levira this month. Allan Allmere, an adviser for IT architecture and infrastructure at the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs, said in comments to POLITICO that Estonia wants to minimize the impact of the worst-case scenario. “Ideally, we would like to build systems that can withstand every possible crisis, but in reality no country can predict or eliminate every risk," he said. "In the most severe scenarios, we also need to preserve a trusted foundation from which Estonia’s digital state can be rebuilt." Advertisement Advertisement The danger to digital services has been apparent for Estonians ever since 2007 when the country faced a wave of cyberattacks lasting 22 days that brought down large swathes of commercial and government services. The country's authorities later attributed the attacks to Russia. The incident was in many ways the first large-scale modern cyberattack targeting a country. It prompted Tallinn to overhaul its entire digital infrastructure, making Estonia what some consider the world's most digitized state. "They have taken a remarkably forward-leaning approach in terms of digitizing government services," said Joseph Jarnecki, senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) think tank in London. Allmere said the doomsday planning seeks to ensure that "we should never have to start again from zero." Digital resilience Recent attacks on data centers in Russia underlined how critical digital services have become for countries at war. Ukraine struck three data centers belonging to Russian provider Yandex last month, showing how targeting compute power had become akin to striking a power plant supplying the electricity, heating and fuel that militaries and civilians depend on. The Estonian national plan for doomsday resilience is a notable example of how countries are looking to protect their citizens and services from those risks through delocalization. Until recently, the debate on digital security tended to focus on keeping control close to home by storing data locally and building technologies and data centers inside a state's territory. Advertisement Advertisement Now states — especially those facing heightened risks of conflict — are rethinking their approach, making sure they are also spreading the risks to digital infrastructure. On Thursday, the United Kingdom and Norway announced they are looking at ways to host each others’ secure data by setting up their own "data embassies." Estonia, too, is investing in "partnerships and alliances with safe third countries" for security and resilience, "rather than saying 'we are most sovereign and most resilient when we have everything physically under our control, within our territory,'" said Jarnecki. The Microsoft outage that struck companies and countries worldwide last week illustrated again how states should diversify cloud and digital service providers in case key providers are struck by cyberattacks, disruptions or technical failures. Allmere, the Estonian official managing the doomsday resilience plan, said the country was also working to prepare for the next challenge: "The first question was how to make sure Estonia’s state data would not disappear," he said, referring to its existing data embassy in Luxembourg as a backup. "The next [challenge] is how to ensure that the state can continue functioning with that data during a crisis," he said. Tallinn won't stop there. "We also need to ensure that the same data remains understandable and usable decades from now," Allmere said. Advertisement Advertisement
